title: Friends of the Rich, a Loan to the LORD
summary: The chapter returns again and again to the poor: better poor with integrity than a fool, deserted by friends and brothers, yet so close to God that kindness to them is a loan to the LORD. Around that theme it gathers sayings on false witnesses, the king's anger and favor, foolish sons and quarrelsome wives, a prudent wife as the LORD's gift, the discipline of children, and the plans of the human heart set beside the purpose of the LORD that stands.
story: The Solomonic collection is nearing its later chapters, and its interest in the social order grows sharper. Chapter 19 looks at who is valued and who is abandoned. Wealth draws friends and poverty scatters them (verses 4, 6-7), and the chapter does not pretend otherwise. But it sets that social reality under God's judgment and care: he repays the lender to the poor (verse 17), and his purpose prevails over every human plan (verse 21). The father's voice also returns directly, addressing my son in verse 27 for the first time since the prologue, a reminder that these sayings are still instruction handed from one generation to the next.
historical:
Verse 17 draws on Israel's laws about lending. The Torah commanded Israelites to lend freely to a poor brother without charging interest (Exodus 22:25; Leviticus 25:35-37; Deuteronomy 15:7-11), and the seventh year brought release of debts (Deuteronomy 15:1-2). Such loans were often never repaid, and a lender could see them as money lost. Proverbs reframes them: the one who is kind to the poor is lending to the LORD, and the LORD will repay.

Verse 26 describes a son who assaults his father or drives out his mother. In a world without pensions, aging parents depended on their children for food, shelter, and protection, and the command to honor father and mother (Exodus 20:12) carried that practical weight. Driving out a widowed mother could leave her destitute. The law treated striking or cursing a parent as a capital offense (Exodus 21:15, 17), which shows how seriously Israel regarded the obligation.
cultural:
Verse 13 compares a quarrelsome wife to a constant dripping, an image drawn from the flat roofs of Israelite houses. Roofs were made of beams covered with branches and packed clay, and in the winter rains they leaked. The drip that never stopped was a familiar misery, and the image returns in 27:15. The saying is not a comment on women in general, since the next verse praises a prudent wife as a gift from the LORD; it is a frank observation about a home without peace.

Verse 24 is one of the book's comic portraits. Meals were eaten by hand from a common dish, with bread used to scoop up food. The slacker puts his hand in the dish and is too lazy to lift it back to his mouth. The exaggeration makes laziness absurd, a technique Proverbs uses often (compare 22:13 and 26:13-15). Verse 12 sets two images side by side: a lion's roar, the most feared sound in the hills of Israel, and dew on the grass, the gift that kept summer crops alive in the dry months.
literary: The chapter is loosely arranged but shows clear threads. Verses 1, 4, 6, 7, 17, and 22 concern the poor, and verses 5 and 9 are almost identical sayings on the false witness, placed like brackets around a group about friendship and wealth. Verse 7 is unusual in having three lines instead of two, and many scholars think its last line is the remnant of another saying whose other half has been lost. Verses 13 and 14 form a pair on wives, one bad and one good, and verses 18, 20, 25, and 27 concern discipline and instruction. Verse 18's second line is difficult: it may warn a parent not to let discipline go so far as to cause a child's death, or, more likely to many interpreters, not to contribute to the child's ruin by failing to discipline at all. Verse 21 restates the theme of 16:1 and 16:9.

outline.t: Integrity, zeal, and folly that blames God
Wealth, friends, false witnesses, and the deserted poor
Fitting order, patience, the king, and wives
Laziness, keeping commands, kindness to the poor, and discipline
Counsel, the LORD's purpose, loving devotion, and the fear of the LORD
The slacker, mockers, shameful sons, and corrupt witnesses

doctrines.note: Many plans are in a man's heart, but the purpose of the LORD will prevail (verse 21). The chapter also warns against the opposite error: a person whose own folly ruins his life and then rages against the LORD (verse 3).

A prudent wife is from the LORD (verse 14), children need discipline (verse 18), and a son who mistreats his parents brings shame (verse 26). Household relationships are where wisdom and folly show most clearly.

Kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD (verse 17). God identifies himself with the needy so closely that what is given to them is counted as given to him, and he takes responsibility for repayment.

words.note: Lavah, to lend or borrow. Verse 17 uses the participle, one who lends, with the LORD as the one who receives the loan. Elsewhere the borrower is the weaker party (22:7), which makes this verse remarkable: God places himself in the borrower's position on behalf of the poor.

Chesed, loving devotion, steadfast love. In verse 22 the BSB reads that what is desired in a man is loving devotion, and the second line adds that it is better to be poor than a liar. Chesed is loyalty that goes beyond obligation, and the saying suggests that such faithfulness is worth more than wealth gained by deceit.

Etsah, counsel, plan, or purpose. In verse 20 it names the counsel a young person should listen to, and in verse 21 it names the purpose of the LORD that stands. The same word covers both human advice and divine intention, and the chapter asks the reader to take both seriously.

Yasar, to discipline, correct, or instruct. The verb is related to musar, discipline. Verse 18 urges a parent to discipline while there is hope, a phrase that stresses timing: correction given early can still shape a life.

christ: Verse 17 is closely echoed in Jesus' teaching. He told his followers to lend expecting nothing in return, promising that their reward would be great (Luke 6:35), and he said that whatever was done for the least of his brothers was done for him (Matthew 25:40). In Proverbs the LORD stands behind the poor as their guarantor; in the Gospels the Son of God stands among them. That is a thematic link, not a prediction, but it is one of the clearest lines from Proverbs to the teaching of Jesus. Verse 21's contrast between human plans and the LORD's purpose reaches its fullest demonstration in the gospel story, where God's purpose to save prevailed through the very plans of those who opposed Jesus (Acts 4:27-28). Verse 11's praise of overlooking an offense describes the patience Jesus taught when he told Peter to forgive not seven times but seventy-seven (Matthew 18:21-22).

hard.q: Proverbs often blames poverty on laziness (verse 15). Is it saying the poor deserve their poverty?
hard.a:
Proverbs does say that laziness leads to poverty, and verses 15 and 24 make the point sharply. But the book never offers laziness as the only explanation, and a reader who takes it that way misreads the collection. Within these chapters poverty also comes from injustice (13:23), oppression by the powerful (14:31; 22:16, 22), dishonest dealing, and plain misfortune. The same chapter that mocks the slacker praises the poor man who walks with integrity above a rich fool (verse 1) and says that kindness to the poor is lending to the LORD (verse 17).

The sayings about laziness are addressed to the young reader as warnings about his own conduct, not as a tool for judging the poor. They tell him that if he sleeps through harvest he will go hungry. They do not tell him that every hungry person slept through harvest. Proverbs describes how life usually goes, and one of the ways it usually goes is that idleness leads to want; it is equally clear that some are poor through no fault of their own and that God defends them.

questions: Verse 17 says kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD. How does this change the way you think about giving that will never be paid back?
Verse 11 says a man's virtue is to overlook an offense. Is there an offense you have been holding that you could let go?
Verse 21 contrasts the many plans of the heart with the purpose of the LORD. How do you make plans while holding them open to God?
